blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Minimal change disease accounts for approximately 80–90% of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in young children in many populations. It commonly responds to corticosteroids.

items.text: S – Small-vessel vasculitis, including IgA vasculitis and ANCA-associated vasculitis.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: A child presenting with cola-coloured urine, facial puffiness, hypertension and oliguria following a recent sore throat should raise suspicion of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

blocks.title: The three major categories of AKI:

items.text: I – Intrinsic renal: Damage to renal tissue.
K – Kidney hypoperfusion from dehydration or shock.

blocks.title: AKI is diagnosed by any of the following:

items.text: Increase in serum creatinine by ≥0.3 mg/dL (26.5 μmol/L) within 48 hours.
Increase to ≥1.5 times baseline within 7 days.
Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for at least 6 hours.

blocks.text: Paediatric clinical pearl: Always calculate urine output in mL/kg/hour. A child with AKI may be non-oliguric, so normal urine output does not exclude AKI.

rows: Lupus nephritis and other systemic disorders

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) are major causes of CKD in children, unlike adults where diabetes and hypertension predominate.
CKD is defined by abnormalities of kidney structure or function persisting for at least 3 months, with implications for health.

rows: Alport syndrome, thin basement membrane disease

Congenital renal and urinary tract abnormalities

items.text: S – Sickle cell disease and trait.
Haemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria, which can produce a positive blood dipstick without true urinary red blood cells.
Dysuria or flank pain, depending on the cause.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Red cell casts strongly suggest glomerular bleeding. Their presence is an important diagnostic clue in nephritic syndrome.

rows: Transient proteinuria following exercise, fever or stress

items.text: Increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier.
Excess circulating low-molecular-weight proteins overwhelm tubular reabsorption.
Examples: haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria and monoclonal light chains (rare in children).
Examples: Fanconi syndrome and tubulointerstitial disease.
Transient proteinuria: fever, exercise, dehydration, seizures and stress.
Orthostatic proteinuria: occurs in the upright position and usually disappears in a first-morning urine sample.
Persistent proteinuria: suggests underlying renal disease and requires evaluation.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: A first-morning urine sample helps distinguish orthostatic proteinuria from persistent proteinuria. Isolated orthostatic proteinuria in an otherwise healthy child is generally benign.

rows: Raised intracranial pressure and autonomic disorders
Renal artery or vein thrombosis, congenital renal disease, coarctation of aorta

Clinical pearl: Renal parenchymal disease is a major cause of secondary hypertension in children. Always measure blood pressure with an appropriate cuff and interpret it according to age.

subsections.subsection_title: 19.8 Causes of Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) in Children

rows: Immature urinary tract defence mechanisms and infant susceptibility

items.text: S – Staphylococcus saprophyticus, particularly in sexually active adolescent girls.
Group B Streptococcus, particularly in neonates.

blocks.text: E. coli is the most common cause of UTI in children.

items.text: C – Cystitis: Infection of the bladder.
U – Upper UTI: Pyelonephritis involving the kidney.
A – Asymptomatic bacteriuria: Bacterial growth without urinary symptoms.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: A febrile infant without an obvious source of infection should be evaluated for UTI. Urine culture is essential for confirming the diagnosis.

items.text: N – Net fluid movement into interstitial spaces.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: In a child with generalised oedema, always evaluate renal function, urine protein, serum albumin, liver function and nutritional status.

rows: Protein loss and poor nutritional status
Renal vein thrombosis, DVT and pulmonary embolism

blocks.text: Encapsulated organisms, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae, are important pathogens.
These occur partly because of urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins and increased hepatic synthesis of procoagulant factors.

items.text: Progressive renal dysfunction in some underlying histological types.
Hypocalcaemia (including reduced total calcium from hypoalbuminaemia).

blocks.title: The three major complications to remember in nephrotic syndrome are:

rows: Due to severe hypertension and fluid overload

items.text: Persistent renal impairment in severe cases.

blocks.text: A child with acute glomerulonephritis who develops headache, vomiting, visual disturbances, seizures or altered consciousness may have hypertensive encephalopathy.
This is a medical emergency requiring immediate assessment and controlled blood pressure reduction.
